title: How do you make collective player agency actually feel meaningful?
author: SkyGlittering2579
selftext:
I'm working on a prototype for an asynchronous narrative game where the whole community rallies behind a single AI character, rather than each player having their own avatar.

The loop is pretty straightforward:  
watch a short story beat → pick a faction or side with a character → chip in resources via a quick mini-game → then see how those resources shape the next episode.

Where I'm hitting a wall is collective agency.

Say you've got 100 players all supporting the same character. Together they gather enough meds, food, or defenses to alter what happens next. At the faction level, the impact is clear.

But on an individual level? I'm not so sure.

If I threw in 20 resources out of a total 5,000, do I actually feel like *I* made a difference? Or does my contribution just vanish into a giant community number?

A few directions I've been kicking around:

* show each player exactly what they personally pitched in
* set resource thresholds that visibly unlock milestones
* give tailored feedback like “your donation helped make XX happen”
* break down bigger faction goals into smaller squad-sized objectives
* let certain contributions unlock specific narrative branches, not just add to a pool

Curious if anyone's tackled something similar.

How would you design a collective progression system so that individual players still walk away feeling like they mattered?

comments.author: Baraga91
comments.body:
Do the populations have to be that big?

If so, divide it into several subtasks, so people can choose which part to interact with. Do I want to add more med packs or do we need more ammo?

Also, make sure that it's always an actual *choice*: if each player has 1 "supply unit", there should be at least 101 units required to completely fill all needs. It makes the players actually be involved, rather than be just a cog in the machine that will eventually reach 100% anyway.

I know we lacked med packs in that last battle, but we needed ammo more... Now I feel bad because lil Joey's leg had to come off :p

replies.author: SkyGlittering2579
replies.body:
Yeah, that's a really good point.

I was overthinking the whole "how do I make each contribution visible" angle, but scarcity might actually fix a bigger chunk of the problem.

If the community can eventually max out everything, then contributing is just filling up progress bars. But if supply never quite covers every need, then every contribution becomes a real choice, what is the group willing to sacrifice?

And I love your Joey example. That's exactly the kind of consequence that makes the next episode actually feel connected to what players did.

One thing I'm curious about is would you show the faction totals live, or hide them until the deadline to push people into making more independent decisions?

comments.author: BansheeTheGame
comments.body:
This feels closer to a reality-show format: end an episode with a vote, then let the consequences play out in the next one. That could make the shared character feel like someone the whole community is collectively steering.

A government-management framing could work too. Players are effectively members of a parliament, and their points represent political capital or time spent pushing a proposal before the vote. That makes individual contributions legible without pretending one person determines the outcome.

replies.author: SkyGlittering2579
replies.body:
Yeah, reality-show framing feels closest to what I'm going for.  
The character still makes their own calls, but the community shapes their situation, like resources, trust, and risk, etc. Players don't need to feel like they single-handedly changed things, just that they helped tip a choice.

  
But how do I avoid it turning into pure majority wins? Should losing-side contributions still leave some trace in the next episode?
